subject: Climate & Environment
title: Wetlands: Nature's Water Filters
description: A fast breakdown of Wetlands: Nature's Water Filters for builders.

hook.text: Wetlands look like muddy wastelands. They are actually among Earth's most valuable ecosystems.

buildup.text: They filter pollutants, absorb floodwater, and recharge underground aquifers naturally.

discovery.text: A single acre of wetland can store over 1 million gallons of floodwater.

twist.text: Humans have destroyed over 85% of the world's wetlands since 1700 — faster than forests.

climax.text: Restoring wetlands costs a fraction of building equivalent water treatment plants.

punchline.text: The best water filter on Earth looks like a swamp.

quiz.question: What percentage of the world's wetlands have been lost since 1700?

details.summary: Wetlands naturally filter water by trapping sediments, absorbing nutrients, and breaking down pollutants through biological processes. They also store floodwater, recharge aquifers, and support extraordinary biodiversity.
details.whyItMatters: Wetlands provide water filtration services worth billions of dollars annually. Their destruction removes nature's most effective water purification system and increases flood risk.
takeaways: Wetlands filter pollutants, sediments, and excess nutrients
They store floodwater and recharge groundwater reserves
Over 35 percent have been lost globally since 1970

faq.question: How do wetlands filter water?
faq.answer: Plants and microorganisms in wetland soils absorb and break down pollutants. Sediments settle as water flows slowly through dense vegetation. Nitrogen is removed through microbial denitrification, and phosphorus binds to soil particles. The result is significantly cleaner water.

faq.question: Can destroyed wetlands be restored?
faq.answer: Yes, though restored wetlands take years to decades to achieve the full functionality of natural ones. Restoration involves rewetting drained areas, replanting native vegetation, and reconnecting hydrology. Many cities are investing in wetland restoration for cost-effective water treatment.
